lead: Denver plumbing deals with cold snaps, expansive soils, basements and century-old brick homes. PipeMend sends licensed local plumbers across Denver.
risk: frozen pipes and sprinkler lines, sewer lines cracked by expansive soil and basement water heaters
risk_short: frozen pipes, sewer lines and water heaters
why: Many Denver homes in Capitol Hill, Baker, the Highlands and Washington Park are more than a century old, with galvanized supply lines, cast-iron stacks and clay sewer laterals. Expansive clay soils along the Front Range move with moisture and crack sewer lines.
Sudden cold snaps after warm days freeze pipes, outdoor faucets and sprinkler backflow devices. Basements hold water heaters, sump pits and floor drains, so basement plumbing is a big share of calls.
water: Denver Water supplies the city with mountain snowmelt from the South Platte and Colorado River basins. The water is relatively soft, so scale is less of a problem than in much of the West, but older galvanized pipes still rust inside.
problems: Capitol Hill, Baker and the Highlands
tips: Blow out sprinkler lines before the first hard freeze.
Scope the sewer line before buying an older home.
Test your sump pump each spring.
areas: PipeMend works in LoDo, Capitol Hill, the Highlands, Wash Park, Cherry Creek, Central Park, Baker, Hampden and every other Denver neighborhood.
permits: Plumbing permits come from Denver Community Planning and Development, and plumbers must be licensed through the Colorado State Plumbing Board.

faq.q: When should Denver homeowners winterize sprinklers?
faq.a: Before the first hard freeze, usually in October. Water left in the backflow preventer and lines freezes and cracks them. A plumber or irrigation pro can blow the lines out.
